one_liner: C++17 parser combinator DSL that beats PEGTL on JSON validation by avoiding implicit backtracking.
what_it_does: lexy lets you write a recursive-descent parser as a C++ DSL built from operator-overloaded rule objects (dsl::), rather than generating one from a grammar file or template-class inheritance like PEGTL. It has no built-in DOM/AST type: results are produced via user-supplied callbacks that write directly into your own types, so integration is closer to 'write a visitor' than 'get a tree back'. Grammars are fully constexpr and can validate, parse into a value, parse into a tree, scan, or trace for debugging using the same rule definitions.
how_it_is_fast: The core idea is explicit, branch-condition-controlled backtracking: rules only backtrack or look ahead when the grammar author says so, unlike PEG engines (PEGTL included) that backtrack implicitly on every ordered choice, re-testing input the programmer didn't intend to re-test. Because output is delivered through callbacks straight into caller-owned types (zero-copy), there's no intermediate DOM allocation/copy step during validation. The library also uses SIMD-width ('SWAR') string/character-class scanning internally (the benchmark's 'lexy no SWAR' variant exists specifically to isolate that contribution).
when_to_use: Validating or parsing well-defined text/binary grammars (JSON-like formats, IPv4/config/protocol grammars) where you control both grammar and target C++ types
You want zero-copy parsing into existing structs/enums instead of building a generic DOM first
You can require C++17 (ideally C++20) and are fine embedding the grammar as C++ rather than an external grammar file
Compile-time (constexpr) parsing of literals/config baked into the binary is valuable
You're already comparing PEG-style combinator libraries and want less implicit backtracking than PEGTL/Boost.Spirit
when_not_to_use: You need a ready-made JSON/XML DOM out of the box — lexy explicitly puts 'implement an efficient container' out of scope, and on the same benchmark page a DOM-oriented library (glaze) beats lexy by ~1.5-2.3x
Pre-C++17 toolchains, or projects that want a small, familiar template-class grammar style (PEGTL) instead of operator-heavy DSL syntax
Teams sensitive to compile-time cost of heavy constexpr/template metaprogramming (author states ~2s per JSON-parser TU in debug; isolate lexy into its own TU)
You need a pinned, independently-run benchmark before adopting on performance grounds alone — this is a first-party nanobench result with no stated compiler/flags
Full parsing into a data structure is the actual workload — the only public benchmark measures accept/reject validation, not construction cost

integration.dependencies: none for the core header-only library (only fundamental stdlib headers like <type_traits>/<cstddef>); a small optional compiled component (lexy_file, from src/input/file.cpp) backs lexy::read_file for file I/O
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake option LEXY_FORCE_CPP17 pins this; uses C++20 automatically when available); CMake >= 3.8 to configure, >= 3.18 for the top-level build with tests/examples/benchmarks
integration.platforms: not documented beyond generic C++17/20 (CI badge present but CI matrix not inspected this session); benchmark hardware was Apple M1 (aarch64), not architecture-restricted
integration.thread_safety: not documented explicitly; core parsing is constexpr/stateless and writes only into caller-provided objects via callbacks, so independent concurrent parses have no obvious shared mutable state, but the docs make no explicit thread-safety guarantee
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same category (PEG-style combinator) as PEGTL but a different DSL style (operator overloading vs templated grammar classes) and a different output model (callbacks into user types vs PEGTL actions), so porting a grammar is a rewrite, not a swap

gotchas: No generic DOM/tree type ships for JSON-like formats; you must define your own value types and callbacks or accept more manual work than nlohmann/rapidjson-style libraries

Grammar rules only backtrack/lookahead where you explicitly write branch conditions — porting PEG intuition from PEGTL/Boost.Spirit (which backtrack implicitly) can silently change parsing behavior, not just performance

Debug-mode compile times are noticeable per translation unit (author-reported ~2s for the example JSON parser); the docs recommend isolating the grammar in its own TU or using dsl::subgrammar to split it

No open GitHub issues surfaced for 'stack overflow/crash/recursion/performance' in a limited search, so no widely-flagged pathological-input bug was found — absence of evidence, not confirmation of safety on adversarial input
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No C++ siblings are catalogued in this category yet (its own baseline, PEGTL, isn't itself catalogued as an entry); relative to the Rust combinators here (winnow, chumsky), lexy targets the same 'combinator beats naive/PEG baseline' niche but the comparisons aren't cross-language-comparable — pick lexy specifically when you're in C++17+, want compile-time grammars, and want less implicit backtracking than PEGTL.
verified_claims_summary: First-party nanobench benchmark (JSON accept/reject validation, no DOM construction) on a 2020 M1 Mac Mini shows lexy beating PEGTL (fetched from its main/develop/master branch at build time, not a pinned release) by ~1.6x-2.2x median latency across canada.json, citm_catalog.json, and twitter.json; compiler and optimization flags are not stated on the page.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2025-10-18, ~1.3k stars) and BSL-1.0 licensed; header-only core makes it easy to vendor, though the DSL is more verbose than PEGTL's and requires C++17.
